papers.title: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.

papers.title: Physics-Spawned Neural Integration of Rotating Shallow-Water Dynamics
papers.abstract: Equation-derived neural integration can execute prescribed dynamics without training, while informative ensemble learning can estimate uncertain parameters and identify governing interactions without requiring differentiability. Together, these approaches motivate Physics-Spawned Informative Networks ($\Phi$SpIN), a framework for prescribed and adaptive hybrid dynamical systems. As a first step toward flood modeling applications, we present $\Phi$SpIN-SW, its prescribed-physics realization for the rotating shallow-water equations. Compatible C-grid operators on spherical Voronoi meshes define a computational graph that retains non-polynomial operations and advances the state through recurrent neural integration compiled with JAX. Analytical benchmarks characterize numerical errors, and global and coastal experiments closely reproduce reference solutions generated using the Model Prediction Across Scales (MPAS) model. At approximately 14~km global resolution, A100, H200 and B200 GPUs attain 9-, 19- and 34-fold higher timestep throughput than a 96-core MPAS-SW CPU reference under matched workloads. These results extend training-free neural integration beyond polynomial dynamics to complex geophysical simulation, establishing a computational foundation for subsequent adjoint-free ensemble estimation of physical and neural parameters and informative adaptation of operator structure.

papers.title: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
papers.abstract: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.

papers.title: Size and shape of condensing steam jets and plumes
papers.abstract: Droplet-laden cloud dynamics emerge from coupled phase transitions and turbulent mixing. Combining experiments and mean-field theory, we establish scaling laws for steam-injected clouds in unsaturated air seeded with condensation nuclei. Depending on whether the cloud is confined to the initial momentum-dominated zone of the jet or extends into the buoyancy-dominated plume, two asymptotic regimes arise. In the momentum regime, cloud dimensions scale with the injector radius. In the buoyancy regime, size follows a $\dot{m}^{2/5}$ scaling, where $\dot{m}$ is the injected steam mass flow rate. Assuming interdroplet air remains humidity saturated, our mean-field analysis predicts cloud persistence governed by enthalpy and humidity mixing. These findings bridge microphysical processes and macroscale dynamics, offering a quantitative framework for atmospheric cloud evolution.

papers.title: On the numerical representation of atmospheric Lamb waves in dynamical cores
papers.abstract: Atmospheric Lamb waves are horizontally propagating acoustic waves that are supported by hydrostatic and nonhydrostatic compressible equation sets. They are classically defined in an isothermal atmosphere and generate no vertical velocity. In a dynamical core, the numerical representation of the Lamb wave is sensitive to modelling choices, such as the upper boundary condition and spatial discretisation. To evaluate the numerical Lamb wave in dynamical cores, we present a new idealised test case that contains a localised pressure perturbation to primarily excite the Lamb wave mode, in a nonrotating, isothermal atmosphere at rest. Lamb waves are identified through their phase speed and the vertical structure of their zonal velocity in three dynamical cores: Spectral Element (SE), Finite-Volume Cubed-Sphere (FV3), and Model for Prediction Across Scales (MPAS), which are available in the Community Atmosphere Model (CAM). Consistent with vertical structure equation theory, the pressure-based coordinate models with an isobaric lid (SE, FV3) generate reduced Lamb wave speeds with low model tops; we show speed reductions of around 25% for a 10 km model top and an isothermal initial temperature of 275 K. For a rigid lid upper boundary condition, such as for the height coordinate MPAS model, the Lamb wave speed is virtually independent of the model top height. Wave amplitudes differ substantially among the tested configurations, with SE producing the largest amplitudes. MPAS' time-adjusted acoustic filter strongly attenuates and broadens the Lamb wave signal, whilst the amplitude and propagation speed are sensitive to the dynamics time step in FV3. Zonal wavenumber-frequency spectra reveal how well the numerical dispersion relations of Lamb and gravity waves follow the theoretical relations, and show element-order-dependent behaviour in SE consistent with linear dispersion theory.

papers.title: GPROF V08: Improving Satellite Precipitation Estimates Across a Heterogeneous Constellation of Passive-Microwave Sensors
papers.abstract: Precipitation estimates from the passive microwave observations (PMW) of the Global Precipitation Measurements (GPM) mission serve a wide range of scientific, societal, and economic applications. The Goddard Profiling Algorithm (GPROF) is the operational retrieval used to produce the precipitation estimates for all GPM PMW sensors. This study presents the implementation GPROF V08 -- the most recent version of GPROF and a major update aimed at improving the accuracy of precipitation estimates from the GPM constellation. GPROF V08 replaces the conventional Bayesian scheme used by earlier GPROF versions by a convolutional neural network (CNN). The first part of this two-part study described a novel ML framework for generating synthetic observations required for training CNN retrievals for all GPM sensors. This second part describes the final, operational implementation, which adds a second finetuning stage to the training.Retrievals from the new GPROF V08 algorithm for all principal GPM sensors are validated against reference precipitation estimates from various sources. Our results show that, while the magnitude of improvements vary by sensor and surface type, they are robust across sensors and metrics and can be as high as 40 \% for the linear correlation coefficient for precipitation estimates from SSMIS and ATMS over ocean compared to combined radar and radiometer retrievals from GPM. While some challenges remain -- such as an increased sensitivity to sensor degradation and the persistence of climatological biases, which remain of the same order as for GPROF V07 -- GPROF V08 constitutes a substantial advancement in spaceborne precipitation monitoring. Since the improvements are robust across all sensor of the constellation, the update is expected to improve the full record of GPM precipitation estimates and thus benefit a wide range of downstream datasets and applications.

papers.title: Twister After Dark: Diagnosing a Damaging Nocturnal Tornado in Iloilo, Philippines (08 August 2026)
papers.abstract: (Abridge) At ~1430 UTC (2230 LST) on 08 August 2026, a significant tornado struck the Mandurriao and Jaro districts of Iloilo City, Philippines. Its parent supercell developed within the southwest monsoon enhanced by Typhoon Dolphin, under weak synoptic forcing, as a nocturnal low-level jet of ~40 kt near 1.5-3 km advected warm, moist marine air onshore. ERA5 depicted MUCAPE of ~2000 J/kg, negligible inhibition, an LCL below 300 m, and nearly purely streamwise low-level vorticity, but deep-layer shear (DLS, 0-6 km bulk wind difference) below 3 m/s. Hodographs from the newly operational Iloilo S-band dual-polarization radar (S-ILO), ~5-7 km from the storm, revealed low-level shear (LLS, 0-1 km bulk wind difference) of ~16 m/s and 0-1 km storm-relative helicity of 124-211 m^2/s^2. The storm exhibited a hook echo with a weak echo hole, a $Z_{DR}$ arc and ring, an elevated 55-60 dBZ rear-flank core consistent with a descending reflectivity core, and a ~50 dBZ ring interpreted as a debris ball. A survey of 31 damage indicators documented a ~2.9 km long and up to ~340 m wide path rated IF2 on the International Fujita Scale. Processor smoothing of the radial velocity and a $\rho_{HV}$ threshold for rainfall estimation masked any tornadic vortex or debris signature, although a radial velocity simulation shows that a narrow vortex (core radius ~50-100 m) with a rotational velocity of ~35-45 m/s could have been concealed. This case shows that significant tornadoes can develop at night during the Philippine monsoon season and that operational radar quality control should be revised to retain severe-storm signatures.

papers.title: Improving Tropical Cyclone Forecasts through Objective Ensemble Track-Error Reduction
papers.abstract: Accurate tropical cyclone (TC) track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning, and risk communication, but outlying members and distinct track scenarios can degrade raw ensemble forecasts. Statistical and machine-learning (ML) methods proposed to improve ensemble guidance are difficult to compare because previous studies often use different forecast systems, basins, periods, and verification methods. Using a common verification framework, this study compares six objective methods (four statistical trimming and two ML methods) with the full ensemble mean for 138 TCs forecast by GEFS, MOGREPS-G, and IFS during 2016-2024. Dynamic trimming (DT) is the most consistent statistical method, reducing mean total track error by 8.0%, 13.4%, and 16.1% at short, medium, and long ranges. Its largest benefits occur in high-spread cases, where it can reach 70% of the low-error bound. Short-lead-error trimming (SLET) provides useful delayed guidance after early observations become available, but its improvement decreases with lead time. Regression-mixture clustering (RC) shows potential in low-spread cases and provides the largest improvement over the control run. The gradient boosted tree (GBT) produces the largest medium-range improvement and exceeds the theoretical trimming bound, suggesting strong potential, particularly when the observed track is poorly represented by the ensemble family. However, its 12.8% short-range degradation and gains concentrated in a small subset of cases indicate overcorrection when the ensemble mean is already accurate, highlighting the need for additional constraints. These results provide a consistent basis for using objective error-reduction methods to strengthen TC track guidance for operational decision-making.

papers.title: Condensation-related expansion work of water vapor as a major pathway for kinetic energy generation in the lower atmosphere
papers.abstract: Earth's atmosphere operates a steam cycle: water evaporates from the surface, expands as vapor, condenses in colder air, and returns as precipitation. Yet its power and relationship to atmospheric mechanical power remain poorly quantified. Applying the Clausius--Clapeyron relation between saturated vapor expansion work and latent heat converted at Carnot efficiency to vertically distributed condensation, we derive the steam-engine power as a sum of the gravitational and condensation-related contributions, $W_v=W_g+W_c$; it is not the net power of a complete moist-air cycle. Using twelve years of GPM/DPR spectral latent-heating profiles and MERRA-2 fields, we estimate $W_v\simeq4.1$ W m$^{-2}$, with $W_c\simeq2.8$ W m$^{-2}$. Separately, we diagnose total atmospheric mechanical power $W=W_P+W_K\simeq4.3$ W m$^{-2}$, comprising gravitational power of precipitation $W_P\simeq1.1$ W m$^{-2}$ and kinetic energy generation $W_K\simeq3.2$ W m$^{-2}$, including $2.4$ W m$^{-2}$ below 500 hPa. Both correspondences $W_v\simeq W$ and $W_c\simeq W_K$ lie within 20--30\% uncertainty estimates. To explain these correspondences, we propose that $W_c$ generates the potential energy associated with surface pressure gradients. Cross-isobaric flow in the frictional lower atmosphere converts this energy into kinetic energy. In a horizontally isothermal atmosphere, this positive pressure work would be nearly cancelled by compression aloft. An idealized circulation illustrates how differential heating can offset compression, allowing nearly isobaric upper return flow. In the proposed mechanism, condensation-driven circulation unlocks this thermal compensation thus providing a major pathway for lower-atmospheric kinetic energy generation. We discuss how changes in the coupling between condensation and differential heating could test this proposed causal relationship.

papers.title: Run it Back: Autoregression vs. Video Diffusion for Final-Conditioned Weather Trajectories
papers.abstract: Low-likelihood, high-impact extremes are projected to increase in severity and frequency in a warming climate. Sampling the precursors that lead to these events traditionally requires massive ensembles that scale poorly with lead time and rarity, and typical rare-event sampling and ensemble-boosting methods do not show how a single extreme might arise from diverse synoptic precursors. Recently, Lin et al.\ (2026) showed this is possible with final-conditioned 66-hour trajectories (trajectories constrained to end at an observed state) from cBottle-video, a pre-trained, off-the-shelf video diffusion climate emulator not explicitly fine-tuned for this task (Brenowitz et al., 2025). However, its ensembles were underdispersed and geostrophically inconsistent, and it reproduces conditioned frames only approximately, hindering autoregressive rollout. Here, we train Rewind-AR, a backward-in-time probabilistic autoregressive model with a FourCastNet~3 backbone (Bonev et al., 2025), and generate final-conditioned ensembles for the same three cases: the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, Hurricane Ian, and Superstorm Sandy (in the Supplementary Information). The leading modes of Rewind-AR's antecedent 500 hPa geopotential height explain far more of the across-member variance than cBottle-video's for both hurricane position and heatwave surface temperature, and Rewind-AR better reproduces the day-over-day heatwave intensification observed in ERA5. Finally, geostrophic inconsistencies close to the conditioning frame seen in cBottle-video are not reproduced by Rewind-AR. Nevertheless, up to 22\% of Rewind-AR members become numerically unstable within 66 hours, so improving rollout physical consistency and stability over long lead times is a natural next step.

papers.title: Community Odour Reports as a Forecastable Sensor of Fugitive Emissions
papers.abstract: Ambient air quality monitors (AAQMs) measure exposure to emissions from waste facilities at few points; for most residents the only record is their own odour reports, used by regulators as evidence of impact but not typically as measurements of exposure. Calibrated public reports are accepted measurements in seismology, but whether community odour reports can serve as a sensor of exposure, and be forecast, is untested against independent monitors. Here we show they can, at a UK landfill, with SENTINEL, which combines the public weather forecast, run through a dispersion model, with the reports already received and no instrument at the site. Judged against the independent monitors, monthly report frequency was correlated with hydrogen sulphide (r = 0.92) and daily reports remained associated with it beyond weather; they fell fourteenfold after a change at the source while modelled transport did not; and, with no gas data as input, gave exposure in both monitored postcodes within a factor of three of that measured. SENTINEL forecast daily report counts with skill 0.64 one day and 0.50 four days ahead, exceeding damped persistence four days ahead; the one-day gain over persistence was unresolved. Community odour reports can act as a relative sensor complementing sparse monitoring; a monitor is needed for absolute scale.

papers.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
papers.abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

papers.title: Short spatial mooring-tilt variations from deep Mediterranean observations
papers.abstract: Interaction between energy-abundant mesoscale eddies and internal waves can lead to convection-turbulence generation and may prove important for deep-sea life and circulation. However, the size of scales of interacting flows is not well known. In this paper, a diagnostic tool of tilt is tested near the single top-buoyancy of 40 mooring lines 9.5 m apart horizontally and compared with 50-m scale relative vorticity and waterflow above a 2500-m deep flat Northwestern-Mediterranean seafloor. Whilst tilt relates to first order with flow-speed squared induced by mooring-line drag, considerable deviations from this relationship and larger tilt occur when the amplitude of relative vorticity attains values O(f), f the inertial frequency of planetary vorticity. The sign of relative vorticity is of no importance. Such larger-tilt events occur during most intense convection turbulence via warm-water slanting from above. During these events, variations in tilt-angle magnitude are as large as the average tilt O(0.1)degr, thereby reducing variational scales from 50 to 9.5 m. Thus, in a deep-sea environment where flow speeds are <0.07 m/s, O(0.01) m/s flow-speed variations provide important turbulent mixing, under conditions without deep dense-water formation.

papers.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
papers.abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

papers.title: A Novel Non-Stationary Bias-Correction Framework for Hurricane Risk Assessment under Climate Change
papers.abstract: Conventional hurricane track generation methods typically depend on biased outputs from Global Climate Models (GCMs), which undermines their accuracy in the context of climate change. We present a novel non-stationary bias correction framework, developed for and applied to the North Atlantic basin, that adaptively accounts for evolving biases in GCM outputs. The framework combines dimensionality reduction with data-driven surrogate modeling to learn the nonlinear evolution between historical and projected GCM climate states, allowing the bias correction to evolve with changing climate conditions. The learned relationship is subsequently applied to a reanalysis-based historical baseline to generate bias-corrected environmental fields under future climate scenarios. Using the empirical Weibull plotting approach, we calculate return periods for wind speed and rainfall across selected North American coastal cities. Our results reveal substantial differences in projected hurricane hazards with and without bias correction, highlighting the importance of accounting for evolving GCM biases in climate-risk assessment and resilience planning. This work highlights the necessity of adaptive techniques for accurately assessing future climate impacts, offering a critical advancement in hurricane risk modeling and resilience planning.

papers.title: Large-scale patterns of small-scale vorticity interactions foster moist convection during cyclogenesis
papers.abstract: Understanding the self-organization of small-scale moist convection at synoptic scales during tropical cyclogenesis is essential. We examine the role of vorticity interactions in dynamical organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis in the Bay of Bengal. Using time-varying complex networks, we encode local vorticity correlations between nodes (locations), only within a spatial proximity of sub-meso length scales. Links are established using short-time correlation of vorticity fluctuations. Spatial patches of high network connectivity depict regions of locally coherent vorticity dynamics. We find that various patches of high network connectivity arrange into extended structures forming identifiable large-scale patterns. Examining the co-evolution of moist thermodynamics parameters with local vorticity coherence, we discover a unique spatial correlation between the convective processes occurring at far away locations, owing to self-organization. We find that such spatial correlation are evident only for depressions that form cyclones, and not otherwise. We discover the physical mechanism of self-organization using modal analysis of network connectivity and vorticity budgets. In regions identified as most influential by the modal analysis, we find that vertical vorticity is enhanced locally as well as advected horizontally outwards to other locations. Such horizontal advection of vertical vorticity induces nonlocal interactions and couples small-scale convective processes across a large domain. We show that, vertical vorticity transported from regions of high convective potential help sustain strong updrafts and weaken convective inhibition in other regions. Thus, spatial interdependence is introduced between small-scale convective processes at different locations, thus explaining the self-organization of moist convection during cyclogenesis.

papers.title: Quantifying internal variability in large-ensemble climate data with the Wasserstein distance
papers.abstract: Estimating forced and internal variability in climate data is fundamental to detecting the climate change signal and assessing uncertainty in climate projections. We propose a metric that quantifies the relative magnitude of internal variability in single-model initial-condition large ensembles (SMILEs). We measure forced and internal variability by two 1-Wasserstein distances, a form of optimal transport cost. The proposed metric is the distance for internal variability divided by the sum of the two. Computing this ratio requires only sorting the samples and differencing the resulting quantiles, with no additional parameters. The metric reflects the entire distribution shape and applies to non-Gaussian variables, because the 1-Wasserstein distance measures the difference between any two probability distributions. We validate the metric with synthetic climate data from Gaussian, uniform, and lognormal distributions. Unlike the two existing metrics, the proposed metric gives stable estimates in the presence of outliers irrespective of the distribution shape, provided that the ensemble has about 40 members or more. We then apply the proposed and existing metrics to the 2 m air temperature and total precipitation of the Community Earth System Model Large Ensemble (CESM-LE) under two different forcing scenarios. All three metrics agree in the spatial pattern of the difference between the scenarios but not in amplitude. The amplitude of the difference is largest for the proposed metric, consistent with the synthetic-data result that this metric changes most rapidly when internal variability dominates. The 1-Wasserstein distance thus provides a simple and useful tool for analyzing large-ensemble datasets.
